Chapter 8: Making Decisions and Taking Consistent Action
So, now that you've tapped into your resourcefulness, the next big step is deciding what to actually do—and then taking action. Ever found yourself stuck, overthinking every option, worrying about making the wrong move? That’s analysis paralysis, and honestly, it can keep you spinning your wheels for way too long.
The best way out? Develop a bias toward action. That means you make the best decision you can with what you know right now—and you just start moving forward. If you need to, you can always adjust along the way. Think of decision-making like steering a boat. You’re not aiming for a perfectly straight line. Instead, you’re constantly making small corrections as things change around you. The real key is movement, not getting stuck or anchored in place.
So, how do you actually get better at making decisions and following through? Here are some steps you can try:
First, clarify your priorities. Figure out what matters most to you right now. By doing that, it’s so much easier to push aside distractions and focus your energy on what’s truly important.
Next, set simple, actionable goals. Don’t just say, “I want to get healthy.” Instead, pick something you can actually do today, like “I’m going to walk for 20 minutes.” Breaking things down makes it way less overwhelming.
And here’s a big one—embrace experimentation. Treat every decision as a little test, not a forever choice. If something doesn’t work out, that’s okay! Adjust and try a new approach.
Remember, consistency beats intensity. Those small actions you take every day? They add up. Imagine learning a new language—you’ll make way more progress by practicing a bit each day, rather than cramming once a month.
Another thing to consider: don’t overload yourself with decisions. Decision fatigue is real, and it can leave you feeling drained and stuck. Try setting up routines and habits, so some choices become automatic. That way, you save your brainpower for things that really matter.
And when you’re facing uncertainty, remind yourself—most decisions aren’t permanent. There’s usually more than one “right” answer. Taking action, even if it’s not perfect, gives you feedback and helps you learn what works and what doesn’t.
At the end of the day, it’s all about bridging the gap between what you want and what you actually do. Making decisions and taking consistent action is how you turn “everything is figureoutable” from just a nice idea into real, tangible progress in your life.
